experiments.title: Retry strategies against a flaky dependency
experiments.question: Which retry strategy rescues orders when 30% of payment calls fail?
experiments.description: Payments answers HTTP 503 to 30% of charge attempts (re-rolled on every attempt) before doing any work, so retrying is safe and the only question is how to retry. Each variant gets the same orders and the same failures.

experiments.title: Retries and double charges
experiments.question: If a charge succeeds but the response is lost, does retrying charge the customer twice?
experiments.description: 15% of charge calls do the work and then drop the connection; another 10% do the work but answer after the client has given up (700ms against a 400ms timeout). The client cannot tell these apart from a failure that did nothing. The payments ledger is the ground truth for how many times each customer was actually charged.

experiments.title: Circuit breakers during a hanging dependency
experiments.question: When payments hangs for 3 seconds, do retries help, hurt, or prolong the outage?
experiments.description: From t+2s to t+5s every payments call stalls for 3 seconds. Payments can only hold 64 requests at once, and a client timeout does not cancel the work already sitting on the server, so abandoned requests keep occupying capacity after callers have given up. Idempotency keys are on everywhere so correctness does not muddy the comparison.

faults.text: payments /charge: adds 3000ms before doing the work, from t+2000ms to t+5000ms

experiments.title: Choosing a timeout
experiments.question: How tight can the per-attempt timeout be before it hurts more than it helps?
experiments.description: Payments normally answers in 20-60ms, but 25% of calls are slow by an extra 450ms. A short timeout abandons slow calls early and retries; a long one waits them out. Every variant retries up to 3 times with idempotency keys.

experiments.title: Queue settings and duplicate shipments
experiments.question: Which queue configuration keeps a shipment from happening twice?
experiments.description: Three things go wrong at once: 15% of acknowledgements are lost, 10% of jobs run slower (1.2s) than a short visibility timeout, and 10% of messages are published twice. At-least-once delivery means all three lead to redelivery. The inventory ledger counts real shipments.

faults.text: worker ack: 15% of requests finishes the job but its acknowledgement never reaches the queue, for the whole run
worker process: 10% of requests adds 1200ms before doing the work, for the whole run
gateway enqueue: 10% of requests publishes the message twice, for the whole run

experiments.title: Queue recovery after a worker outage
experiments.question: After the whole worker tier is down for 3 seconds, how long until the backlog clears?
experiments.description: Each shipment job takes about 150ms, and orders arrive at 10 per second. The worker tier is down from t+2s to t+5s while orders keep arriving. Work in flight at the moment of the crash is abandoned un-acknowledged, so it only comes back when its visibility timeout expires, and the backlog that built up during the outage has to be worked off by however many workers there are. Recovery means the last order shipped late (more than 1s after the customer was told 'accepted') has shipped. Compares visibility timeout and worker count.

worker *: is down (connection refused), from t+2000ms to t+5000ms
